subject: HIS
label: Grade 11 Humanities
task: Meet the outcome of every unit in Grade 11 Humanities History, and keep one piece of evidence for each.
condition: A 36-week school year, 4 units, a teacher or guide, a learning book or device, and local examples in the local language first with English support.
standard: Each unit: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown. Course pass: no unit at 'Not yet' after one retry, and a pass in SA1 and SA2.

modules.title: From the beginning of time to early societies
modules.intro: In this unit you work on 'From the beginning of time to early societies', taught in a way that is with exam-style questions and written reasoning. The target is clear: describe early human societies. You move from seeing it, to saying it, to doing it alone.
points: Place it: find where and when 'From the beginning of time to early societies' happens, on a map, a timeline or in a local example.
Gather: read or listen to two short sources and note who is speaking and why.
Use it: describe early human societies. Give a reason and one piece of evidence for every point.
Weigh it: say what another person might think, and why, before you decide.
modules.example: Solved: Take one source or data set. Ask five questions: who made it, when, why, what does it show, what is missing? Write three sentences using one piece of evidence each, then say what other source you would check. Method: Model run for 'From the beginning of time to early societies'. Question: what happened, or what is the situation, and why? Sources: two short extracts, a map or table. Notes: who, what, where, when, why. Answer: three sentences, each with a reason and a piece of evidence. Check: is there a point of view that you have not considered? What a good answer looks like: facts are correct, reasons are linked to evidence, and one other point of view is named fairly.
modules.activity: About 40 to 50 minutes of class work, then one short practice task for home. Keep evidence: a timed paper and an error log.
modules.standard: Describe early human societies: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Describe the timescale first. Current evidence suggests modern humans appeared in Africa roughly 300,000 years ago, while farming began only about 10,000 years ago. So farming covers about 3 percent of our species' time, and for the rest people lived by hunting and gathering. Draw a line and mark both dates.

Step 2, Describe hunter-gatherer societies. Small bands of perhaps 20 to 50 people moved with the seasons, gathered plants, hunted animals, made stone tools and used fire for warmth, cooking and protection. Our evidence comes from tools, bones and cave paintings, not from written words.

Step 3, Describe the shift to farming. From about 9500 BCE in West Asia people grew wheat and barley and kept sheep and goats. In South Asia the farming village of Mehrgarh dates from about 7000 BCE. Settling brought storage, surplus food, larger villages and new ideas of property.

Step 4, Describe the first cities. Uruk in Mesopotamia had grown into a city by about 3500 BCE, with temples, officials and traders, and cuneiform writing appeared by about 3200 BCE. Surplus food freed some people to become potters, priests and scribes. Name three signs of a city: size, specialist work and record keeping.

Step 5, Explain how we know. Archaeologists dig in layers, with older objects lower down, and date organic material by radiocarbon, which reaches back around 50,000 years. A stone scraper suggests hunting, while a grinding stone suggests farming. Always state what the evidence cannot show, such as beliefs.

Step 6, Your turn: describe two differences between a hunter-gatherer band and a farming village. Answer: a band moved with food and owned few things, while a village stayed in one place, stored grain and grew larger, so farming villages could develop surplus food and specialist work.

modules.standard: Compare empires and their legacies: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Choose criteria before you compare: size, government, economy and legacy. Take three empires, Rome, Han China and the Mauryan empire of India. A comparison works only when each empire is judged on the same points, so write them as column headings in a table.

Step 2, Compare lifespans using dates. Han China lasted from 202 BCE to 220 CE, which is 202 + 220 - 1 = 421 years, since there is no year zero, counting a short break in the middle. The Mauryan empire, about 321 to 185 BCE, lasted about 136 years. The Roman Empire in the West, 27 BCE to 476 CE, lasted 502 years.

Step 3, Compare government. Rome ran provinces under governors, spread citizenship and used written law. Han emperors relied on salaried officials chosen for talent and loyalty. The Mauryan capital at Pataliputra controlled provinces through royal officials. Write one sentence on each, noting how it kept control.

Step 4, Compare economy and links. Roman paved roads and sea lanes joined the Mediterranean world. Han China sent silk westward along the routes later called the Silk Road. Mauryan roads linked the northern plains to the coasts, and punch-marked silver coins helped trade. Note which empire relied most on roads.

Step 5, Compare legacies. Roman law and Latin shaped later European law and languages. The Han left the model of a unified state run by trained officials. Mauryan inscribed pillar edicts, in local scripts, are among the earliest public writing in South Asia. Rank which legacy lasted longest and explain why.

Step 6, Your turn: compare how Han China and Rome held their territory. Answer: Han China used salaried officials answerable to the emperor, while Rome used provincial governors, legions, roads and the spread of citizenship; both depended on taxes and a strong army to keep control.

modules.standard: Explain religion, trade and learning across regions: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Explain the routes first. Goods and ideas moved on overland Silk Roads and by sea across the Indian Ocean. Sailors used the monsoon: the southwest wind in summer carried ships from Arabia to India, and the northeast wind in winter brought them back, so a round trip fitted in one year.

Step 2, Explain how religion travelled with trade. Merchants carried silk, spices and cotton, and also their beliefs. Buddhism spread from India along oasis towns of Central Asia and reached China by about the first century CE. Monasteries beside the routes gave travellers rest, so trade and religion supported each other.

Step 3, Explain the spread of learning. Indian numerals and the zero were taken up by scholars writing in Arabic in the eighth and ninth centuries, and later reached Europe. The word algebra comes from the Arabic al-jabr. A translation movement in Baghdad turned Greek, Persian and Sanskrit works into Arabic.

Step 4, Explain the spread of technology. Paper came from China and was being made at Samarkand by the mid-eighth century, then spread west. The earliest dated printed book, a Buddhist scroll from China, is from 868 CE. Cheaper paper and printing made books easier to copy and share.

Step 5, Explain causes and effects in a chain. Cause: rulers wanted trade taxes and protected roads. Effect: merchants travelled widely. Result: religions, numbers, paper and crops moved across regions and mixed with local cultures. Write each link with because or so, and avoid claiming one cause explains everything.

Step 6, Your turn: explain why religions often spread along trade routes. Answer: merchants and travellers moved along the routes, stopped in towns and monasteries, and shared their beliefs with the people they met, while rulers and traders who valued safe trade supported those centres.

modules.standard: Describe revolutions and industrialisation: at least 70 percent on an exam-style task, with the method shown.
steps: Step 1, Describe the age of revolutions with a timeline. The American Declaration was in 1776, the French Revolution began in 1789 and the Russian Revolution came in 1917. The gaps are 1789 - 1776 = 13 years and 1917 - 1789 = 128 years. Mark each on a line and say what changed in each.

Step 2, Describe the French Revolution. Causes were royal debt, high bread prices and an unequal system of three estates. On 14 July 1789 a crowd stormed the Bastille prison in Paris. The 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen stated that men are born free and equal in rights.

Step 3, Describe industrialisation. It began in Britain from about the 1760s, where textile machines, coal, iron and the steam engine moved work from homes into factories. Early public railways opened in 1825 and 1830. Say why Britain led: coal and iron nearby, capital, and overseas markets.

Step 4, Describe the social effects. Factory towns grew fast with crowded housing, long hours and child labour. The Factory Act of 1833 banned children under nine from working in textile mills. Describe one gain, cheaper cloth, and one cost, poor living conditions, to give a balanced answer.

Step 5, Link industrialisation to the wider world. Mills needed raw cotton and new markets. Britain imported raw cotton from its colonies and the United States, and sold machine-made cloth abroad. In India this harmed hand-loom weavers, which shows how industry in one region changed life elsewhere.

Step 6, Your turn: describe two effects of steam power on transport. Answer: steam locomotives made rail travel faster and cheaper, with passenger lines from 1825 and 1830, and steamships allowed regular sea crossings that did not depend on wind, so goods and people moved farther in less time.

ladder: L1: talk about family, place and community.
L2: read maps and timelines; describe local government and history.
L4: analyse causes and consequences; argue from evidence.
L5: specialise in history, geography, politics or economics; write extended answers.
L6 (degree): research methods and applied social science.
L7 (postgraduate): policy, research or teaching at depth.
